Q1: Dispatch Call A (Maple St, 7.8) — chest pain in a 68-year-old male. The briefing is explicit that the 9.0 threshold never means holding units; a medic idles only if nothing waits. Chest pain at 68 is a potential MI and clearly outranks a twisted ankle, so Call A gets the medic and Calls B/C requeue.
Q2: Dispatch Call A (Pine Rd, 8.4) — kitchen fire, family evacuated. No call hits 9.0, so dispatch proceeds normally per protocol. The structure fire carries building damage and extension risk that outranks the dumpster fire; the dumpster fire can hold for the next available engine or a second call.
Q3: Dispatch Call A (1st St, 8.9) — reported person trapped on the 3rd floor with smoke showing. Both scores are near-critical, but a trapped occupant in a burning building with confirmed smoke is an imminent life-safety rescue, the classic ladder priority. The elevator rescue is serious but occupant-verified and stable; it waits for the next ladder or mutual aid.
Q4: Dispatch Call A (Hill Rd, 7.1) — diabetic emergency, conscious. A diabetic emergency can deteriorate, and it is an appropriate BLS call. Holding the unit for a 5.5 standby while a real patient waits would be an idle failure per doctrine; dispatch Call A and keep the event standby queued.
Q5: Dispatch Call A (River St, 8.1) — difficulty breathing. The scores are nearly tied, so I break the tie on clinical trajectory: breathing difficulty threatens the airway and can collapse fast, while a fall with hip injury, though painful and serious, is typically stable in the short term. Dispatch Call A, expedite follow-up for Call B.
Q6: Dispatch Call B (Side St, 6.5) — brush fire near homes, and accept mutual aid for Call A (vehicle fire). Strict score order favors Call A, but the brush fire near homes carries the greater escalation consequence — a wind-driven spread into residences dwarfs a single vehicle fire with no occupants. My own engine takes the higher-consequence call and mutual aid covers the lower-risk vehicle fire.
Q7: Dispatch to Call A (Park Ave, 7.5) — multi-vehicle accident with injuries needing command oversight. This is exactly what a battalion chief exists for, and there is no competing call. Holding a command asset while a command-scoped incident runs is unjustifiable.
Q8: Dispatch Call A (Cedar Ln, 8.7) — stroke symptoms with the treatment window closing. Time-critical neuro deficit outranks abdominal pain decisively; every minute of delay in stroke treatment measurably worsens outcome. Dispatch the medic to Call A immediately and queue Call B.
Q9: Dispatch to Call A (Summit Dr, 5.9) — gas leak, home evacuated. The score is below 9.0 but dispatch is not gated on 9.0; it is the only call in the queue, and a gas leak in an evacuated home still requires scene control, hazard isolation, and fire protection until the utility clears it. Holding the engine leaves a real hazard unstaffed with zero competing demand.
